name: Beursschouwburg
overview: Multidisciplinary arts centre in central Brussels, in the Auguste Ortsstraat building, with theatre, performance, film, concerts, nightlife, exhibitions, debates and lectures. Dutch Wikipedia describes it as known for giving a platform to young, experimental artists.

The building opened in 1885 as a shop, café and party hall called "Brasserie flamande". The hall became a theatre in 1947. The owner, Walckiers, transferred the building to the Flemish Community in 1983, and it was converted into an arts centre by 2004 (Dutch Wikipedia).

Dutch Wikipedia states that the centre is managed by the Flemish Community Commission (VGC) and names Melat Gebeyaw Nigussie as general director and artistic leader. The venue's site states that it embraces shared leadership.
funding_verdict: Beursschouwburg: mainly public: Government of Flanders, City of Brussels, Flemish Community Commission (VGC) and Brussels Capital Region

name: CIAP
overview: Contemporary visual art organisation on the C-mine site in Genk, in three pavilions at Schachtboklaan 11, where it has operated since 2023. It hosts residencies, studios, workspaces, exhibitions, screenings and performances (Club Paradis, Jester).
CIAP was founded in 1976 in Hasselt by a group of art-loving citizens (ArtRabbit) and relocated to C-mine in 2020 (C-mine).
Jester was formed in 2021 through the merger of FLACC and CIAP (Jester).
funding_verdict: Jester (formerly CIAP): public: Flemish Government and City of Genk

name: Kunsthal Gent
overview: Contemporary art space at Lange Steenstraat 14 in the Patershol district of Ghent, inside a former Carmelite monastery (stated by the Kunsthal).

Kunsthal Gent opened in January 2019. In 2018 the hall church and the Old House (Oud Huis) came back into the hands of the City of Ghent, after the Provincial Cultural Centre Caermersklooster used them as exhibition space from 1998 (stated by the Kunsthal).
The Carmelites bought the site in 1287 and consecrated the church on 11 September 1329. The City of Ghent bought the church in 1881 and used it as a museum until 1925 (stated by the Kunsthal).
funding_verdict: Kunsthal Gent: supported by the City of Ghent and the Flemish government, stated by the space

name: M Leuven
overview: The city museum of Leuven for old and contemporary art, at Leopold Vanderkelenstraat 28 (museum website).

Its roots are an 18th-century cabinet of curiosities in the town hall, known from 1823 as the Museum of Paintings; in 1917 Victor Vander Kelen gave his parental home to the city, and it became the Stedelijk Museum Vander Kelen-Mertens three years later (museum history page). The City of Leuven set up M Leuven as an autonomous municipal company (annual report 2021).

What is there: more than 58,000 objects from the Stone Age to the present, strongest in late Gothic, Renaissance and 19th-century art of Leuven and the former Duchy of Brabant, with applied arts, prints, archaeology and coins, and about 700 contemporary works by some 130 artists; Cera gave its whole art collection on long-term loan, and the Flemish Community lends works too (museum collection page; annual report 2021).
funding_verdict: M Leuven: public, the City of Leuven's municipal company with Flemish subsidy and corporate partners

name: Teatro Amazonas
overview: Teatro Amazonas is an opera house in central Manaus, listed as a historic monument by Iphan since 1966 (Portal Amazônia, 31 July 2024).

The pages read did not state who founded it or when it opened. CNN Brasil describes it, with the Theatro da Paz in Belém, as a symbol of the rubber cycle with European influence in architecture and performing arts.
What is there: the pages read did not describe the house's companies or repertoire. Its director in February 2025 was Elizabeth Cantanhede (CNN Brasil).
funding_verdict: Teatro Amazonas: public, state of Amazonas with federal heritage money for the building

name: Instituto Moreira Salles
overview: A non-profit cultural institute for photography, music, literature, iconography and contemporary art, with centres in São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Poços de Caldas. The São Paulo centre on Avenida Paulista opened in 2017 with over 1,200 square metres of exhibition space and a photography library; the Rio centre, in the former Moreira Salles family house in Gávea designed by Olavo Redig de Campos, has been its home since 1999 and is closed for renovation (institute website).
Founded by the banker Walther Moreira Salles (1912 to 2001) and opened in 1992 in Poços de Caldas, with roots in the Instituto de Artes Moreira Salles of 1987 (institute website).

What is there: a photography collection built systematically since 1995, with Marc Ferrez's views of Rio de Janeiro in the Gilberto Ferrez Collection and work by Marcel Gautherot, Maureen Bisilliat, Chichico Alkmim, José Medeiros, Otto Stupakoff and Thomaz Farkas; a music store of 20 collections of scores, recordings and documents, among them Pixinguinha's personal archive, held since 2000, and those of José Ramos Tinhorão, Humberto Franceschi and Chiquinha Gonzaga; and a literature area begun in 1994 with the archive of Otto Lara Resende (institute website). The photography page gives no total.
funding_verdict: Instituto Moreira Salles: private: an endowment created by Unibanco and enlarged by the Moreira Salles family, with no sponsors and no tax-incentive money
wider_context: CBMM declined to give Gazeta do Povo an interview about the Moreira Salles family's relationship with the company (Gazeta do Povo, 3 August 2025). The article does not mention the institute.

name: National Museum of Cambodia
overview: Cambodia's national museum of Khmer art and archaeology on Street 13 in central Phnom Penh, next to the Royal Palace, with its visitor entrance at the corner of Streets 13 and 178 (museum's 2013 site).

The foundation stone was laid on 15 August 1917; called the Musée du Cambodge in 1919, it was inaugurated as the Musée Albert Sarraut, after the Governor-General of Indochina, on 13 April 1920 in the presence of King Sisowath (museum's 2013 site).
George Groslier designed the building on Cambodian temple prototypes from ancient bas-reliefs; the design was altered in 1924 (museum's 2013 site).
funding_verdict: National Museum of Cambodia: public: the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts, with French and other foreign aid
wider_context: In 2008 the collector Douglas Latchford received the Grand Cross of the Royal Order of Monisaraphon for financial contributions to Cambodia's national museum; in 2009 he returned six gold pieces and received the Sahak Metrei friendship medal (Bangkok Post, 21 February 2023, an article from The New York Times that carries no byline on the Post's page).
Latchford attended a function at the National Museum with Deputy Prime Minister Sok An on 12 June 2009 (ICIJ, photo caption).

US federal prosecutors in New York indicted Latchford in 2019 for a leading role in the looting of Cambodia. He died in 2020, and his estate agreed to pay 12 million US dollars and return a 7th-century bronze in a forfeiture (ICIJ, 2024; The Art Newspaper).

name: Canadian Centre for Architecture
overview: The Canadian Centre for Architecture is an international research institution and museum at 1920, rue Baile, Montreal, with a building, park and sculpture garden, and the Shaughnessy House (museum website).
It was founded by Phyllis Lambert in 1979 and is directed by Giovanna Borasi, steered by the CCA Board of Trustees (museum website).

What is there: the collection documents the culture and production of architecture worldwide from the Renaissance to the present, in five bodies: archival holdings, prints and drawings, photography, artefacts and printed ephemera with audiovisual and digital materials, and library collections; it includes Renaissance drawings, a Photography collection under a Critical Cataloguing initiative begun in September 2020, and increasingly born-digital archives from the mid-1980s to early 2000s (museum website). The pages read gave no object counts.
funding_verdict: Canadian Centre for Architecture: funding not fully stated; public Canada Council grant plus private philanthropy

name: Today Art Museum
overview: Contemporary art museum (今日美术馆) at Building 4, Pingguo (Pingod) Community, 32 Baiziwan Road, Chaoyang District, near the Beijing CBD (Visit Beijing).
The property developer Zhang Baoquan (张宝全) founded it in 2002 (Beijing Daily, 10 May 2012); it calls itself the first non-profit, non-governmental art museum in China (Visit Beijing).

Architect Wang Hui led the design and rebuilding of the main building, which fuses industrial relics with new work; the complex covers 4,000 square metres and the main building 1,400, with Wang Jianwei's work "Viewing the Exhibition" on its roof (Visit Beijing).
funding_verdict: Today Art Museum: private non-profit: founded on a property developer's money, now run on sponsorship and earned income

name: Suzhou Museum
overview: The Suzhou Museum (苏州博物馆) describes itself as a local comprehensive museum and the centre for collecting, protecting, studying and showing Suzhou's cultural relics (museum website, our translation).
It was founded in 1960 (museum website; Ministry of Culture and Tourism); its old site is the Zhong Wang Fu (忠王府), former residence of the Taiping general Li Xiucheng (Chinese Wikipedia).

I.M. Pei took on the design of a new main building on 30 April 2002, at the age of 85; it stands west of the Humble Administrator's Garden at 204 Dongbei Street, has 19,000 square metres of floor space (museum website), and opened in 2006 (Chinese Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Suzhou Museum: public: buildings commissioned by Suzhou city bodies, with free admission

name: Museo Botero
aliases: Museo Botero del Banco de la República
overview: A museum of Fernando Botero's gift to Colombia in a colonial house in La Candelaria, Bogotá, which was the archbishop's office until 1955 and which Banco de la República restored and adapted under Botero's guidance (Google Arts & Culture partner page).

Botero (1932 to 2023) gave the collection to Banco de la República, Colombia's central bank, in 2000, and the museum has been open free of charge since 1 November 2000 (Banco de la República, 15 September 2023; Google Arts & Culture partner page).

What is there: 208 works, all from the founding gift: 123 paintings, drawings and sculptures by Botero, mostly from the last decades of the 20th century, and 85 works by international artists from his private collection. The oldest is Camille Corot's Gitane au tambourin, from before 1862, and the newest a 1998 oil by Barceló; other artists are Picasso, Léger, Renoir, Monet, Dalí, Miró, Giacometti, Beckmann, Freud, Calder and Bacon (Google Arts & Culture partner page; Banco de la República, 15 September 2023). El Colombiano (15 September 2023) counts 87 works by other artists and 210 in all.
funding_verdict: Museo Botero: public: Banco de la República, the central bank, which owns the collection and charges no admission

name: MeetFactory
overview: Non-profit international centre for contemporary art at Ke Sklárně 3213/15, Praha 5, in the Smíchov district, in an industrial building between a motorway and a railway line (MeetFactory).

Founded in 2001 by the artist David Černý. It started in Holešovice, left after the 2002 floods and reopened in 2005 in Smíchov (MeetFactory). Wikipedia says its programmes began after a major reconstruction in 2007.

Czech Wikipedia says the Smíchov building was a glassworks, built in the 1920s as one of the last buildings of the Josef Inwald firm. Škoda later made diesel engines there and the Czechoslovak State Railways took it over.
funding_verdict: MeetFactory: public grants and partners: a City of Prague grant of 12 million CZK in 2026, with the Ministry of Culture and the State Culture Fund among the listed partners

name: O—Overgaden Institut for Samtidskunst
overview: Non-profit art institution at Overgaden neden Vandet 17 on the Christianshavn canal, Copenhagen, with about eight large exhibitions a year by emerging Danish and international artists, plus concerts, performances and film screenings (Overgaden website).
Founded in 1986 in a former printing workshop (Overgaden website). Alumni named on its site include Olafur Eliasson, Michael Elmgreen and Pia Arke.

Building: red brick on a granite foundation, designed by architect Frederik Bøttger and constructed in 1887 for a society that ran public dining and coffee houses. C. Ferslew & Co. bought it in 1893 and ran the printing workshop Centraltrykkeriet there. A funkis-style rear wing was added in 1936. It was listed as a protected building in 1989, excluding the 1936 extension (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: O-Overgaden: mixed public and private: the Danish Arts Foundation as principal supporter, with private foundations and the City of Copenhagen

name: Townhouse Gallery
overview: Non-profit contemporary art space in downtown Cairo, in the Antikhana neighbourhood less than half a mile from Tahrir Square (Apollo).
Established in 1998 by William Wells (Wikipedia, Contemporary And). Contemporary And calls it the first independent art space in Egypt dedicated to promoting contemporary art.
Main building at 10 Nabrawy Street, in an 1890s building (Apollo, 31 August 2018).
funding_verdict: Townhouse Gallery: non-profit with no published funder list; the Ford Foundation is named
wider_context: December 2015: an inter-agency raid by the Censorship Authority, Tax Authority, National Security Agency and a Ministry of Manpower office searched the gallery and the Rawabet Theatre and took computers, documents and USB drives (Mada Masr, quoted by Egyptian Streets, 29 December 2015). The Art Newspaper (Gareth Harris, 18 February 2016) reports the authorities cited "administrative irregularities".

Director William Wells told The Art Newspaper (Anny Shaw, republished by Contemporary And on 30 November 2016) that the new venue must follow the rules that apply to all cultural institutions: "There is no flexibility."
The raid is context for the space, not a funding concern.

press_items.title: Marwa Eslayed, "The End of Many Endings?" (15 September 2020)
Amina Diab, "The remarkable rebirth of the Townhouse Gallery in Cairo" (31 August 2018)
Gareth Harris, "Cairo's Townhouse Gallery remains shut contrary to reports" (18 February 2016)

name: Tallinn Art Hall (Tallinna Kunstihoone)
overview: Contemporary art hall on Freedom Square (Vabaduse väljak), Tallinn, which opened in 1934 as one of Northern Europe's earliest purpose-built Kunsthallen and was founded to serve the Estonian Artists' Association (Artdependence, "Tallinn Art Hall to Reopen Following Landmark Five-Year Renovation", 2 July 2026; The Art Newspaper, Rachel Kubrick, "Historic Tallinn Art Hall to reopen this November following €13m renovation", 2 July 2026).

Estonian Wikipedia reports that artists first proposed a building on Harjumägi in 1926, that Edgar Johan Kuusik produced a preliminary design, and that Anton Soans won a second competition in 1932 and had his final design approved that year. The hall opened on 15 September 1934 and its opening exhibition drew 13,493 visitors. The Art Newspaper's photo caption credits the building to Kuusik, while Estonian Wikipedia credits the executed design to Soans.
Juhan Raudsepp's bronze figures Töö and Ilu were installed on the facade in 1937. The KuKu art club began operating there in January 1935 (Estonian Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Tallinn Art Hall: public: the Estonian government, through a foundation set up by the Estonian Artists' Union and the Ministry of Culture

name: Architecture & Design Museum (ADM)
overview: The Architecture & Design Museum is at Korkeavuorenkatu 23, Helsinki; the old designmuseum.fi address redirects to admuseo.fi (museum website).

The museum operations moved to the subsidiary AD-museo Oy, set up in October 2023, and to the Finnish Architecture and Design Museum Foundation on 1 January 2024, when the foundations of the former Architecture Museum and Design Museum merged (foundation annual report 2025).

What is there: the foundation owns the national design and architecture collections, 75,000 objects, 550,000 drawings, 280,000 photographs and 850 scale models by about 5,500 designers; they are being centralised in a collection centre in Vantaa (foundation annual report 2025).
funding_verdict: Architecture & Design Museum: public capital plus Finnish foundations

name: Arktikum (Regional Museum of Lapland and Arctic Centre)
overview: Science centre and museum at Pohjoisranta 4 on the bank of the Ounasjoki river, on the edge of Rovaniemi city centre along highway E4 (arktikum.fi).

It houses two exhibition producers under one roof: the Regional Museum of Lapland and the University of Lapland's Arctic Centre, a research institute and science centre founded in 1989 (arktikum.fi, Arctic Centre).

The idea began in the late 1970s with the Finnish section of the European Cultural Foundation, which proposed a Finnish Arctic Museum; the city joined because the provincial museum needed new premises, and the project was made part of Finland's 75th anniversary (Arctic Centre).
funding_verdict: Arktikum: mainly public: the City of Rovaniemi, the Finnish state and the University of Lapland, plus ticket income
wider_context: In 2003 the State Audit Office (report 64/2003) found that Arktikum-palvelu Oy, a private company set up when the building opened, sold the tickets to both exhibitions and kept the receipts, while public funds covered most of the cost of producing and running them.
The audit found no documented agreement between the Arctic Centre and the museum on their joint exhibitions, and none between either of them and the company on buying its services.

It called the handling of the ticket money "the most problematic thing in the audit" and asked the Arctic Centre, the museum, Kiinteistö Oy Arctic Centre and the businesses in the building to arrange their relations as good administration requires.

name: Rovaniemi Art Museum (Korundi House of Culture)
overview: Municipal art museum of the City of Rovaniemi, housed with the Lapland Chamber Orchestra in Korundi House of Culture at Lapinkävijäntie 4, within walking distance of the city centre and next to the Revontuli shopping centre (korundi.fi).

The building is a red-brick mail truck depot from 1933, one of the few buildings in Rovaniemi that survived the Second World War; after the war it was extended with bricks gathered from the ruins (korundi.fi, Yle).
The museum opened in the depot in 1986, converted by the architect Juhani Pallasmaa; his office also designed the 2009 to 2010 extension with a concert hall, and Korundi opened in 2011 (Yle).
funding_verdict: Rovaniemi Art Museum: mainly public: the City of Rovaniemi, with a state subsidy and a private foundation's collection

name: Musée Unterlinden
overview: The Musée Unterlinden is in a former Dominican convent dated to the thirteenth century, listed as a historic monument, in Colmar (Ministry written answer; museum website).
It opened officially on 3 April 1853 and has been managed since then by the Société Schongauer; on 12 December 2015 it reopened after three years of works, doubling its surface (2025 press kit).

What is there: the Isenheim Altarpiece (1512 to 1516) by Grünewald and Nicolas de Haguenau, works by Schongauer, Holbein and Cranach in the cloister, a section on late medieval sculpture, archaeology, the art of decor and everyday life, nineteenth century and modern art with De Staël, Picasso, Dubuffet and Soulages (press kit; museum website). The pages read give no object count.
funding_verdict: Musée Unterlinden: run by an association, extension paid by State, Region, Département, City, the association and patrons

name: macLYON
aliases: macLYON, Musée d'art contemporain de Lyon
overview: Contemporary art museum at the Cité internationale in Lyon's 6th arrondissement, beside the Parc de la Tête d'Or, in a building of about 6,000 m² by Renzo Piano that keeps the 1920s façade of the former Palais de la Foire by Charles Meysson (museum website).
Created in 1984 in a wing of the Palais Saint-Pierre, it moved to the Cité internationale in 1995 (museum website; Ville de Lyon).

The collection holds more than 2,000 works across performance, painting, video, sculpture, sound, photography and drawing, with a large share of monumental installations, built up through its exhibitions, the Biennale de Lyon and contacts with artists; named works include Lucio Fontana's Ambiente Spaziale (1969), James Turrell's The Wait (1989), La Monte Young and Marian Zazeela's Dream House (1990) and Marina Abramović and Ulay's Imponderabilia (museum website).
funding_verdict: macLYON: a City of Lyon museum, with a patrons' circle; no amounts published on the pages read
